title: API Security: BOLA, BFLA and mass assignment
description: API-exclusive attacks per OWASP: reading other users' objects, running admin functions and promoting yourself with one extra JSON field.

1.title: BOLA: other users' objects
1.body:
## The most common authorization bug in APIs

Authentication answers "who are you?" (valid token → alice, id=2).
**Authorization** answers "can you touch THIS?" — and that is the one that fails.

```bash
# Who am I?
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:18101/api/me
# {"id": 2, "name": "alice", "role": "user"}

# Which orders exist? Enumerate IDs:
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:18101/api/users

# ANOTHER user's order (user_id: 1 = admin):
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:18101/api/orders/1002
# {"id": 1002, "user_id": 1, "amount": 999.99, ...,
#  "note": "BOLA: this order belongs to user 1 but you are user 2"}
```

The server looks the order up by ID and returns it. It never compares
`order.user_id` with the token's `id`. Change `1002` to `1001` or `1003`
and you walk through every order in the store: addresses, amounts,
items. In real APIs (banking, healthcare, government) this single bug
leaks millions of records with a `for` loop over consecutive IDs.

## Exploiting it with a script (like a real attacker)

```bash
for id in 1001 1002 1003; do
  curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:18101/api/orders/$id" | grep -E 'id|item'
done
```

The classic web-app IDOR is exactly this under another name:
BOLA is the API version of IDOR.

## The fix

```python
order = orders.get(oid)
if order['user_id'] != current_user['id']:   # ← the missing line
    return error(404)  # 404 and not 403: don't reveal that it exists
```

Even better: queries that already filter by owner
(`WHERE id = ? AND user_id = ?`) instead of fetching first and checking afterwards.

2.title: BFLA, mass assignment and unlimited consumption
2.body:
## BFLA: admin functions within reach of a DELETE

BOLA was "seeing what you shouldn't". **BFLA** (Broken Function Level
Authorization) is "doing what you shouldn't": the API exposes administrative
functions and only checks that you are logged in, not your role.

```bash
# Alice (role: user) deletes bob:
curl -s -X DELETE http://127.0.0.1:18101/api/users/3
# {"status": "deleted", "user": "bob", "note": "BFLA: you should not be able to do this!"}
```

The classic symptoms in real APIs: admin endpoints mounted on the
same host as the user ones (`/api/admin/users` forgets the role
middleware), HTTP method collisions (the DELETE reaches the same route as the public
GET) and "hiding" the button in the frontend with no validation in the
backend.

## Mass assignment: the field you gave away

When the backend does `role = body.get('role', 'user')` — or worse, passes
the whole JSON to the model constructor — any field you send
becomes yours:

```bash
curl -s -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": "mallory", "role": "admin"}' \
  http://127.0.0.1:18101/api/orders/create
# "MASS ASSIGNMENT: you set role=admin!"
```

The most famous exploit in history was exactly this: in 2012, a
researcher added `"admin": true` to the JSON of his GitHub profile...
and became an admin of the platform.

**Fix**: an explicit allowlist of acceptable fields (`name`, `email`)
and never map the body straight onto the model (in Django: `ModelForm` with
declared fields, not `**request.POST`).

## Unlimited resource consumption

`/api/export` has no rate limit, no pagination and no special
authentication: a single GET downloads ALL users and ALL orders.
An attacker can bring your database down (and run up your bandwidth bill) with
a `while true`.

```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:18101/api/export | jq '.flag'
```

The standard mitigations: rate limiting per IP and per token (429),
mandatory pagination (`?page=1&limit=50`), response size
limits and per-user compute "budgets". In paid APIs,
also: quotas per API key.

## How a real API is audited

1. Enumerate the endpoints with the spec (Swagger/OpenAPI) or with Burp.
2. For EACH endpoint ask yourself: someone else's object? (BOLA) a function of
   another role? (BFLA) an extra field in the body? (mass assignment)
   a usage limit? (resources).
3. Always test as a LOW-role user: the admin sees everything and
   masks the bugs.

api-security-t02-q01.hint: curl -X DELETE http://127.0.0.1:18101/api/users/3 — deleting users is an admin function, but the API doesn't check the role
